The Nancy Grace Roman Telescope: Eyes Wide Open

Equipped with an unprecedented field of view and remarkable infrared precision, the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is poised to scan the Universe on a scale never before achieved. Its mission? To unravel the mysteries of dark matter and dark energy—these two constituents that account for a staggering 95% of the cosmos, yet remain largely misunderstood.

Set for launch by NASA on August 30, 2026, the Roman telescope features a field of view that’s one hundred times greater than Hubble’s. With its lightweight mirror, innovative optical design, and a coronagraph to hunt exoplanets, this mission brings technological feats by the dozen. The ultimate goals? Mapping dark matter, exploring dark energy, and paving the way for the search for habitable worlds.

Dark Matter & Dark Energy: The Great Unknown

Not less than 95% of the Universe escapes us completely. Dark matter and dark energy—two invisible entities whose nature and composition remain unknown—still manage to dominate the dynamics of our cosmos. To mark the launch of the Roman Space Telescope, we interviewed Alain Blanchard, an astrophysicist specializing in cosmology, to get his uncompromising perspective on what we do (and especially do not) know about these cosmic puzzles.

Alain Blanchard: “It’s an interesting question, and in many ways, it comes down to personal bias… The three possibilities you’ve brought up are indeed the three main lines of thought one might consider.”

There’s certainly no shortage of candidates to explain dark matter: WIMPs, axions, primordial black holes, or even modified gravity theories like MOND (Modified Newtonian Dynamics). But so far, none has provided direct evidence. When it comes to dark energy, the mystery only deepens—theoretical predictions for this force accelerating the Universe’s expansion differ from observations by… well, 120 orders of magnitude. Yes, you read that right: 120 zeroes.

Shadows and Light: Tensions, Theories, and Beyond

Add to the mix some real tensions in the standard cosmological model—like the famous “Hubble tension”—which might signal anything from a minor tweak to a seismic shift in our understanding of the cosmos.

Alain Blanchard speaks candidly, weaving together scientific rigor and philosophical curiosity. From the true nature of dark matter to the tensions shaking the standard cosmological model, from the destiny of our Universe to the philosophical consequences of these discoveries, his insights offer a captivating, sometimes unnerving, snapshot of modern cosmology.

Alain Blanchard: “Of course. MOND is an alternative theory with its own supporters, even if it causes a bit of a schism… Recently, with an intern, we showed that MOND doesn’t correctly reproduce the rotation curve of our Galaxy as measured by Gaia. Our ‘MONDian’ colleagues reacted swiftly, but I wasn’t convinced by their arguments (and they weren’t published in accepted journals, unlike our work).”

Blanchard notes that these theories introduce new exotic entities—”fields”—tweaked just enough to reproduce what the standard model predicts. “So, we’re making up ‘things’ that look like dark matter, smell like dark matter, taste like dark matter but aren’t dark matter…”

Initial conditions become crucial, often tailor-made to achieve the desired result. As Blanchard observes, neutrinos have mass and thus contribute, at least a little, to dark matter—but it’s insufficient and, for now, largely unobservable.

Mapping the Universe: Where Roman, Euclid, and Gaia Meet

Both ESA’s Euclid mission and Roman, operating at the Lagrange point L2, are designed to study dark energy and dark matter—each with complementary methods. Euclid will survey about 15,000 square degrees (nearly a third of the sky) in both infrared and optical wavelengths, though with less detail than Roman. Roman’s main survey, deeper and more precise, will cover a smaller area: 5,100 square degrees, around 12% of the sky. Its high-precision infrared vision will show the cosmos as it was two billion years ago, revealing even more faint galaxies.

Where their observation zones overlap, scientists can use Roman’s superior data to correct and extend Euclid’s findings to a much broader swath of the sky.

And the detective work goes on: Recent findings from the European Gaia satellite (which precisely measures the motions of countless stars in our galaxy) have seriously challenged MOND and provided further evidence in favor of dark matter, as Blanchard and his colleague Even Coquery shared in interviews.

Alain Blanchard: “Everything is possible because if [dark energy] evolves, we don’t know why, and so it could evolve in the future in a way we can’t foresee—transform into classical dark matter (which is the ‘natural’ way if you extrapolate naively), or head towards a ‘Big Rip’. There isn’t any option we can exclude. Even with every instrument imaginable, there will always be a margin of uncertainty in its properties. That means a Big Rip could come later, or it might behave like matter, or radiation, or as something we’ve never seen…”

Philosophically, Blanchard points out: “What makes up most of our cosmos is of a different nature than us (meaning, it isn’t atoms)—and its precise nature, in the end, may not be so important?”

The ratio between dark matter and dark energy shifts over time, being insignificant in the early Universe and likely to overwhelmingly dominate in the distant future. Why are we living at just the right period to witness this transition? Blanchard notes, “Weinberg had ‘predicted’ this situation…”

What he awaits most—particularly from ESA’s Euclid Space Telescope—is confirmation or refutation of whether dark energy varies over time. Current data hints at it, but isn’t yet decisive.

Naively, says Blanchard, it’s hard to expect a revolution from Roman or Euclid, as they are designed to refine what’s already been measured quite accurately. But a theoretical breakthrough—well, that’s another story. Remember Mercury’s misbehaving perihelion? A small deviation in Newton’s law, not enough to discard Newton’s theory, but perfectly explained by Einstein’s general relativity, which then opened up a century of new predictions and confirmations.

Blanchard suspects the standard “LCDM” cosmological model might share this fate: a very good approximation of something entirely new, without the endless adjustments that plagued the old “epicycle” theories, which were less wrong because of their predictions and more because each new observation required yet another tweak.
